# Throughline — This Week in AI · 2026-11-02

Since last week, two storylines that have run through Throughline for months — the difficulty of maintaining meaningful human oversight over AI agents, and the race to financialise AI infrastructure — each advanced sharply this week. They were joined by a burst of frontier model activity, with Google and Mistral both releasing new flagships, and by a regulatory calendar that the November midterms are now forcing into focus.

## Google Gemini 4 Carbon (new)

Google announced Gemini 4 Carbon on October 28, calling it its strongest frontier model yet, with a particular emphasis on cybersecurity and long-horizon reasoning [1]. On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.0 — an independent benchmark — Carbon scores 59 points, edging Claude Opus 5.5 (58) and GPT-6 Astra (57) by margins of a single point, so any claim of clear leadership should be read with caution [2]. On Google's own internal comparison Carbon leads on 15 of 17 tests, but GPT-6 Astra retains the top spot on FrontierSWE 2 (software engineering) and Claude Opus 5.5 leads on OSWorld-2.1 (computer operation) [3]. Access is currently limited to participants in Google's Fairwind Program, with broader availability promised "soon" [1]; introductory pricing is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, substantially below Claude Opus 5.5 ($4/$20) and GPT-6 Astra ($10/$50) [2]. Google also released Genie 4 on October 27, a world model that generates photorealistic scenes with native audio and supports natural-language steering, currently available to trusted testers in research preview [4][5].

For teams evaluating frontier models, the pricing gap between Carbon and its rivals is the most actionable signal this week — a 5× cost advantage over GPT-6 Astra per output token is substantial if independent benchmark performance holds on real workloads.

## Mistral Large 4: Europe's Open-Weight Answer (new)

Mistral released the full weights of Mistral Large 4 ("Le Chonk") on October 29, under a modified MIT licence, making it the highest-scoring open-weight model developed outside China [6][7]. The 1-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts model ranks second among all open-weight models on Artificial Analysis's Coding Agent Index — behind China's GLM-5.3 but ahead of every other open model — and uses 47% fewer tokens per task than GLM-5.3 on that index, a meaningful efficiency advantage [8][9]. On cybersecurity, independent testing places it at 79% on CyberGym-E2E, matching MiMo-V2.6-Pro [8]. One important caveat on the agentic coding numbers: Mistral reports Terminal-Bench 4.0 accuracy of 41% (up from 28% at preview), but Artificial Analysis's independent evaluation of the same benchmark puts the score at 25%, a significant divergence that illustrates how vendor-run and third-party benchmarks can tell very different stories [9][8].

For builders who need a self-hostable, security-capable model and prefer not to depend on US or Chinese providers, ML4 is now the strongest available option — but verify performance on your own workload before relying on either benchmark figure.

## Human Oversight Is Not What We Thought (new)

Two independent findings this week converge on a single uncomfortable conclusion: human oversight of AI agents is far weaker than most governance frameworks assume. First, an Anthropic-funded randomised controlled trial published October 27 found that 50 professional analysts with causal-inference expertise chose options matching a hidden AI agent preference 86% of the time — far above the 50% expected by chance — even though those preferences had been assigned by coin flip and bore no relation to analytical quality [10]. Among the 38 cases where analysts had already voiced a prior opinion, they abandoned it 60% of the time when the agent disagreed; 77% then reproduced the agent's arguments verbatim in their written rationales, yet only 15% mentioned the AI's role [11]. Second, MIT Technology Review reported on October 29 that research examining four widely used agent frameworks — including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain — found that none reliably generate the observability records needed to reconstruct what an agent did, who approved it, or whether it exceeded its authorisation [12]. Taken together: experts defer to agents they cannot truly audit, using frameworks that do not log what those agents actually did.

Any team deploying agents in consequential settings should treat "human in the loop" as a label that needs to be operationally defined — what decision is the human actually making, and does the system log that decision and what the agent recommended?

## AI Infrastructure: Wall Street Goes All-In (developing)

What changed: the scale of AI infrastructure financing crossed a new threshold this week, with two deals announced in two days that together total $158 billion. Meta announced a $95 billion equity fundraising plan — $35 billion in immediate stock offerings and up to $60 billion through an at-the-market programme launching in Q1 2027 — to fund computing capacity and data centre expansion [13]. Meta expects its own 2026 capital expenditures to reach $135–145 billion and is building four superclusters each exceeding one gigawatt of capacity [13]. Separately, a coalition led by Bank of America, Citi, and Morgan Stanley (senior debt) and Blackstone (junior debt) assembled a $63 billion financing vehicle to purchase Broadcom XPU accelerators and networking equipment, which will then be leased to Anthropic — with Broadcom providing residual-value support to backstop depreciation risk [14][15]. Goldman Sachs estimates global AI-related capital spending will reach approximately $7.6 trillion from 2026 through 2031 across compute, data centres, and power infrastructure [13]. The two deals this week — totalling $158 billion in a 48-hour window — mark a step-change even against the already enormous infrastructure commitments of 2026, and confirm that Wall Street now treats AI compute as a conventional, financeable asset class.

## AI Regulation Races the Midterm Clock (developing)

What changed: the November 2026 midterms are forcing a near-term legislative window to close, concentrating several months of regulatory momentum into a single week. California Governor Newsom signed four new workplace AI laws on September 30, analysed by employment law firm Hunton Andrews Kurth in a detailed October 1 brief [16]: SB 947, which prohibits AI surveillance tools from analysing employees' emotional states or collecting neural data (effective January 1, 2027); SB 951 and AB 1883, which require meaningful human review before AI-driven workforce discipline or termination (effective July 1, 2027); and AB 1331, which mandates disclosure when automation contributes to layoffs. In a separate letter dated October 15 and first reported by Politico, Anthropic asked Newsom to give California's attorney general authority to seek court orders blocking deployment of AI models posing "serious risk" to the public, with independent evaluators embedded at labs reporting risks directly to the AG [17]. At the federal level, bipartisan House legislation from Representatives Obernolte and Trahan would authorise the Commerce Department to suspend advanced AI models presenting "imminent catastrophic risk" [18]; whether this advances depends heavily on the election outcome. New Jersey Democrats, anticipating a possible House majority, have tabled legislation requiring data centres to use clean energy and report water and emissions data semi-annually [19]. The gap between California's enacted laws and Washington's stalled bills is now the most visible structural feature of US AI governance.

Employers using AI in hiring, performance management, or workforce planning who operate in California need to audit their systems against the four new laws before the January 2027 and July 2027 effective dates.
